Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00173

The objection assumes that a soul without a body has no power to imagine. But this is not true of souls that are still incomplete or midway in their development. They may be free of material bodies but remain connected to image-like forms. If the objection means that they are free of sense bodies but remain connected to such images, there is no problem. We will explain this in the discussion of the afterlife. The soul can have particular, image-based perceptions and a power of imagination that arises from its own being, because, as we said earlier, the soul itself has hearing, sight, inner perception, and the power to move.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00174

Its power to act and its power to perceive are one in its unified existence. Its ability to move belongs to its ability to perceive; its imagination belongs to its inner sight. All the outer powers are shadows of aspects that exist together in the soul's own being. In this life, they have separated and multiplied, stretching into the matter of the body and taking the shape of its organs. In itself, the soul has sight, hearing, taste, smell, touch, and the active power to present what it perceives directly, as if it were present before it.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00175

Our knowledge and imagination in this life are seeds of direct vision in the next. The difference between imagining something now and seeing it there is a difference in strength. The soul encounters whatever it longs for. If its thoughts and images in this life have been good, kind, and pure, they become gardens, satisfaction, peace, fragrant plants, and angels to keep it company in this life and bring it joy in the next. If they have been evil, ugly, and false, they become snakes, scorpions, fires, a wrathful keeper of Hell, and devils. They harm the soul in this life and distress it in the next.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00176

The argument that an unlimited number of souls would have to gather on one body does not apply. First, the discussion concerns only the souls of the miserable, not every soul. Second, some souls do not connect to bodies, while others connect to image-like forms. Even if their number were unlimited, they would not crowd one material body. Image-like forms do not compete for one material place, so their number need not be limited. There is therefore no need for the number of those forms—or of material bodies—to be either finite or infinite in the way the objection claims.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00177

I am surprised that some people who are said to understand divine truths and look toward the lights of the heavenly realm—such as the author of The Intimations—could accept the idea that a celestial body is the basis for the images of groups of happy and miserable souls. Their souls, they say, have not reached the intellectual world and have not broken their ties to bodies; they remain potentially intellects and need a bodily relation. The author calls this a good explanation. Yet elsewhere he rejects the idea that the souls of the miserable could be attached to noble celestial bodies with luminous souls. He says that their potentiality requires bodily images, and proposes a solid, spherical body beneath the Moon and above the sphere of fire, serving as an in-between realm for their imagined fires, stinging scorpions, snakes, and bitter fruit.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00178

He says that this account answers the remaining objections to transmigration. He adds that, based on his own spiritual exercises, he is certain that ignorant and sinful people would reach the greater spirit if they were freed from a bodily power that recalls their states, preserves their ignorance and traits, and shapes their images.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00179

But a soul's imagining something through a celestial body, or another kind of body, requires a direct relation to it or a relation through something that is directly connected to the soul. The soul would have to be the form that completes that body, through its own being or through one of its own powers. In short, the soul would have to act on the body in some way. At the very least, the body would have to act as a surface or mirror does for some perceptions: it would need a positional relation to the material body that receives the soul's actions and is the basis for its powers.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00180

A celestial body, however, is not acted on by anything separate from its own source. As we said earlier, the heavenly bodies are not affected by anything other than their own intellectual sources, and cannot receive strange, forced influences from outside.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00181

Those who say that celestial bodies host the images of separated souls give those souls no bodies that could have a positional relation to the celestial bodies. The soul's relation to a celestial body would depend on its natural relation to its own body. Once death ends the natural relation to the body, the dependent positional relation must also end. When the root is gone, so is the branch. Their account is therefore false.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00182

Moreover, if the celestial body were like a mirror for the soul's images, the images would be the ones already present in that body, formed by its own soul—not images created by the souls of the dead. It is impossible for a celestial body to receive dark and painful images unlike those its own noble soul forms. A pure receiver can take only true images from a noble source. The unhappy souls are tormented by their own bad traits, false images, and corrupt beliefs, not by images that match reality. So the account does not work.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00183

The same problem applies to the proposed special, created body whose kind exists only in one individual, placed below the Moon. It would have to be a fifth kind of heavenly nature, even though it was said to be beneath the Moon. It would also be finite and smaller than the Moon. If the number of miserable souls is without limit, how could all of them use that one body for their endless images? At the very least, the body would need an unlimited capacity, which is plainly impossible.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00184

The truth, as we have established, is that the images that delight the happy and torment the miserable in the next life exist in another realm, not in a material body or a bodily power. They exist in their own right, and the souls of the happy and miserable reveal them through their own activity. The images that appear in a mirror are not part of the mirror; the mirror reveals them by receiving them. It is possible for the soul to create something through one aspect of itself and to be affected by it through another. The soul has an intellectual, active side and a natural, receptive side. Just as its activity can produce health or illness in the body and the soul then feels pleasure or pain from them, so its actions produce the good or bad images that follow from its obedience and disobedience, and it experiences delight or pain from them. These two aspects are present in the soul before it becomes pure intellect. At that stage, it acts and perceives through one side, as we have explained before.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00185

Everything that reaches the soul in the next life comes from what it has brought forth. Souls that are not complete in knowledge and action, or only in knowledge—whether they are middling in happiness, incomplete in both knowledge and action, incomplete in knowledge, or miserable—may be free of earthly matter and natural bodies but remain attached to afterlife images. These images give delight or pain more intensely and last longer than changeable earthly bodies. The Qur'an says, “The punishment of the next life is harsher and lasts longer.” Even the fire and pain of this world are effects of the fire and punishment of the next life, or the same thing in a diminished, clouded, and weakened form. The Prophet is reported to have said that our fire is part of the fire of Hell, washed seventy times and then sent down to this world. The same is true of light: earthly delight is small compared with the delight of the next life.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00186

Here is a reminder that further supports this view and explains why the afterlife images that bring the happy delight and the miserable torment do not exist in celestial or other bodies. They are image-forms belonging to the soul, present in another realm, and produced through actions and deeds in this life. Those deeds shape habits and character in the soul, and those in turn bring about the images.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00187

Ibn Arabi, a leading authority on spiritual unveiling, says that the realm of images in which spirits dwell after leaving this world is not the same as the realm between separate spirits and bodies. Existence descends and rises in a circle. The realm before earthly life belongs to the descent and comes first; the realm after earthly life belongs to the ascent and comes last.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00188
Ibn Arabi also says that the forms spirits encounter in the final realm of images are the results of their past actions, unlike the forms of the first realm.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00189
The two realms share the fact that they are spiritual and luminous, not material.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00190

He explains elsewhere that the first realm is called the “possible unseen,” because what is there can appear in the visible world. The second is called the “impossible unseen,” because what is there cannot return to this earthly world, except in the next life. Few people have direct insight into that second realm; many can see or gain knowledge of the first and learn what events may occur in the earthly world. He also says that a person may see, in sleep and after death, qualities that are usually temporary appear as independent forms that speak to them. They may seem like bodies carrying spirits, and the dreamer or the dead person has no doubt that they are real. Someone with direct insight can see while awake what the sleeper sees in a dream and what the dead person sees after death. In the next life, a person sees forms of actions, even though actions are normally passing qualities; death itself may appear as a white ram, even though it is the separation of things that were joined.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00191

Some people perceive these images through the senses while awake; others perceive them through imagination. In dreams, they are certainly perceived through imagination. Ibn Arabi also says that after death, in the imaginal realm, people perceive things through the same images they had in this life. Each person there is held by what they have earned, confined within the forms of their actions until the resurrection in the next life.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00192
IV. How the soul relates to the body, and the difference between natural death and death from an outside cause
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00193

Know that the soul carries the body; the body does not carry the soul, as most people think. They hear that the soul is the product of the elements and the balance of bodily qualities. They suppose that the soul comes from the body, grows stronger when the body is nourished, and grows weaker when it is not. This is mistaken. The soul brings the body into being and gives it its form. It moves the body in different directions. The soul is present with the body, its powers, and its limbs, guiding them as it wills and taking them wherever it wishes. It can move the body down or lift it up, despite the body's heaviness. When the soul wants to lift it, the body rises and its heaviness gives way to lightness. When it wants to lower the body, it moves down and its lightness gives way to heaviness.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00194

But the soul cannot rise to the heavenly world, the home of spirits and the blessed, or to the highest dwelling place with this dense body. It rises with a body of light, of the same kind as that world, after leaving behind this dark bodily frame. And the soul cannot rise to the home of those brought near to God, or to the realm of perfect beings and separate intellectual forms, until it has left behind the limits of bodies and dimensions, detached itself from images and shapes, and risen beyond both worlds.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00195

The point is that the soul is too exalted, in its journey through these realms, to depend on the body for its existence. At some lower stages, the body is instead one of the things that depend on the soul. This principle disproves both transmigration and the view that natural death happens because the body runs out of strength, loses its inborn heat, wears out its tools, and falls apart, as many doctors and natural philosophers have thought.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00196

The truth is that the soul gradually becomes independent in its existence. Little by little, it leaves this natural life for another kind of life. As we have explained, the very being of material things is in motion. The soul changes from one state to another and grows stronger in its existence. As it grows stronger, it gives less of its power to the body, because its attention is turning elsewhere. The body and its powers then grow weaker and wither in a natural way. When the soul reaches the limit of its strength and independence, it completely ends its connection with the body, its care for it, and its giving of life to it. The body's death follows. This is natural death. It is different from death brought on by an outside accident.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00197

The body's decline after the age when growth stops, followed by old age and death, comes from the soul's changes as it approaches the next life: a life in which it is on its own, apart from this natural body and this world, and exists independently. The bodily stages we see in a person—childhood, youth, gray hair, old age, and death—follow corresponding stages in the soul, but in reverse. As the soul gains strength and becomes more fully itself, the body grows weaker and less able. At last the soul stands on its own and the body dies. The soul's departure brings the body's ruin; the body's ruin does not cause the soul to depart.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00198

A poet puts it this way: “The soul meant to leave. I said, ‘Don't go!’ It answered, ‘What can I do? The house is falling down.’” That saying applies to death caused by an outside accident, not to natural death. In general, people have not understood the soul's return journey toward God, a journey we have shown to be present in most things. They have therefore offered mistaken explanations of death. What we have explained also shows why this death is called natural, rather than for the reasons they give.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00199

What we have said does not deny that some souls are miserable, or that they will suffer in the next life in Hell, in fire, and under God's anger. They will face these things as payment for their deeds and the results of their actions, bad habits, and false beliefs. We will explain this more fully later.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00200

Once we understand that natural death begins when the soul turns by its nature toward the next life and draws near to God, we can see that every kind of transmigration is impossible. After the death of its earthly body—whether its life ended naturally or through an outside cause—the soul cannot enter another natural body or move from one body to another. If it moved into another body, it would have to enter at the body's beginning, when it was a drop of fluid or an embryo in the womb, as supporters of transmigration admit. This would contradict what we have established: the stages in the soul's growth and the body's growth move together in reverse. Remember this, traveler on the path to God.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00201

Use your insight to see that from the day you came into being as a drop in a safe place, you have been moving toward your Lord. You have passed from a lower state to a better one, from a less complete stage to a higher and nobler one. You will continue until you meet your Lord, see Him, and have your deeds weighed. Then you will remain with Him, either joyful and at peace forever, among the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the good—excellent companions—or grieving, suffering, and punished by God's blazing fire, which reaches into the heart, among unbelievers, devils, evildoers, and hypocrites. What terrible companions they are.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00202

We have already explained that all things in this world are moving toward God, though most do not know it because their veils are thick and their darkness has piled up. In a human being, this inward journey is clearer, especially in the complete human being who travels the whole upward arc, from creation back to God. Those with direct insight know this: their inner sight is not covered by blind imitation, doubt, desire, or attachment to this world. This is God's favor, which He gives to whom He wills.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00203

The human body in this world is like a well-built ship at sea, carrying many powers and workers that serve it by God's permission. A ship can move from place to place only when the wind of its will blows. When the wind dies down, the ship stops. “In God's name it sails and comes to rest.”
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00204

If the wind, whose relation to the ship is like the soul's relation to the body, stops, the ship comes to a halt before any part of it breaks or any tool fails. In the same way, when the soul leaves, the human body and its organs can no longer sense or live, even if its limbs and bodily matter have not yet decayed. What has gone is the breath of life, like the wind that moved the ship.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00205

The proof is clear: the wind is not part of the ship. The ship's movement follows the wind; the ship does not carry the wind. By God's permission, the wind carries and moves it, and it sails in God's name. Those on board, with all their different powers, cannot bring the wind back by a trick or a device. The same is true of the soul and its life-giving breath. They are not made from the body's substance, and the body does not carry the soul. No bodily power or mixture of bodily qualities can bring the soul back once it has left.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00206

This example shows that the body's life and movement follow the soul; the soul does not follow them. It also disproves transmigration, which claims that a soul can return to a body after leaving it, because that body's mixture and material are ready to receive it. As we have explained, the soul itself preserves the body's balance, brings its parts together, and keeps its elements joined. The soul follows no bodily mixture or elements.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00207

The difference between natural death and death from an outside cause can also be shown by the ship. A ship can be destroyed in two ways. First, its hull can be damaged or its structure can come apart. Water then enters, and the ship sinks with everyone aboard if they have failed to notice the damage and repair it. The body and its powers can likewise be destroyed when one bodily quality overwhelms the others, because a person has neglected the body. When its balance is lost, its order breaks down, its parts are no longer in proper proportion, and its tools grow weak, the soul no longer remains with it. The wind, however, has not vanished; it remains in its own source, just as the soul remains in its own realm after the body is destroyed. This is death from an outside cause.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00208

The second way a ship can be destroyed is when a violent wind strikes it with a force that the ship and its tools cannot bear. The tools weaken and break because they cannot withstand the force. So too, when the soul grows stronger in its very being and its inborn heat grows more intense, the body can no longer bear it. Its structure breaks down, its tools dry up, and its moisture is used up as the heat takes over.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00209

In our view, the inborn heat of old people is stronger than that of the young. Its effect is less visible because the body that carries it is weaker and its material has dried up. This is the opposite of the common view that older people have less heat than the young. Natural death, then, comes from heat overpowering the body and consuming its moisture. The body's own heat finally fails, and death follows. This is a necessary result of the soul's own growth and purpose. Here, that purpose is the soul's strength and perfection: the spirit becoming more complete, and the life-giving breath growing stronger. In the ship's example, this is like a storm whose force overwhelms the ship.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00210

The people on this ship, caught in such a storm, respond in one of two ways. If they understand God's plan, they are at peace and surrender themselves to Him before the veil is lifted. As they leave this world, they urge one another to be patient, not to despair, and to look with longing toward the home they are about to reach. Once they understand this divine order and work with it through reason and faith, their grief and worry come to an end, and they reach lasting happiness.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00211

But if they do not understand God's plan—that all that the Wise One does is good and right—and do not accept the call to trust and surrender, their reward is Hell. They are kept from happiness and far from the pleasure of God, the All-Knowing and All-Wise.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00212
V. Every person has one self: the soul itself is the living, perceiving, and thinking being
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00213
It is also the being that hears and sees, nourishes and grows, and reproduces. In a sense, it is the natural body that moves, grows, and senses.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00214

We have already proved this in earlier chapters, but we want to explain it more fully because it matters greatly to understanding how all actions come from the First Reality. Each of us knows, before reasoning it out, that our self is one thing, not many. At the same time, we know that we are the one who thinks, perceives, senses, desires, becomes angry, occupies space, moves, and rests. We are described by many names and qualities. Some belong to reason and thought, some to sensation and imagination, and some to the body and its states and reactions.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00215
This is something we know directly. Yet most people cannot recognize it through careful study and deny that the self is one when they begin to investigate—except those whom God has given light.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00216

If someone cannot see the unity of their own self, how can they see the unity of their Lord? The early thinkers divided different actions among different powers. They assigned each action to a different power, then had to explain whether one power among them was the source and the others depended on it. Let us review the views reported on this question and the arguments for each.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00217

Some said there is one soul. They disagreed about how its powers work. Some said the soul performs its actions through different bodily tools, with a particular action coming from each power. This is the view of Avicenna and those in his school. Others said that the soul is not one: the body has several souls, some for sensation, some for thought, some for desire, and some for anger.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00218

Those who deny that the soul is one argue as follows. A plant has a power for nourishment, while an animal has powers for nourishment and sensation, but no power for thought or reason. Since a plant's nutritive soul exists without an animal's sensitive soul, and an animal's sensitive soul exists without a rational soul, they say these must be different souls. If one soul did all these things, they argue, each power would have to be present whenever any one of them was present.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00219

They also say that since these powers are separate in some beings, they must be separate souls when they are found together in a human being. But this argument is weak. Some simple kinds of thing contain different features in one and the same existence. For example, one feature may be present where another is absent. That does not prove that the features have separate existences in the thing they form.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00220

Also, the nutritive power in a plant is not the same kind of power as the nutritive power in an animal. Nor is the sensitive power in a nonthinking animal exactly the same kind as the sensitive power in a human being. They share a broad meaning, like “able to sense,” when we consider that meaning on its own, apart from the other things that complete it.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00221

When “able to sense” is complete and independent, as it is in animals other than humans, it is already a full kind of living power. It does not wait for another power to complete it. But when it can become real only by being joined to something more complete—such as the rational power in a human being—it is different in kind, even though the two share a broader meaning. So the sensitive soul in other animals is different from the human soul that can think. In a human being, they are one. The same applies to the nutritive power in plants and the nutritive power in animals and humans. Remember this rule; it will help you.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00222

Those who say the soul is one argue that we have already shown that different actions of the soul come from different powers. Each power, in its own role, can produce only a certain kind of action. The power of anger is not moved by pleasure, and the power of desire is not affected by painful things. The power that perceives is not affected in the same way as either of them.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00223

These powers can sometimes work together and sometimes oppose each other. When we sense something, we may desire it or become angry. But if we focus on thought, our senses may grow weaker; if we focus on sensation, our anger or desire may grow weaker.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00224

If there were no shared source to direct all these powers, they could not cooperate or conflict in this way. For each power has its own tool, and its actions are not linked to the actions of the others. If there is a shared source, it must be a body, something present in a body, or something that is neither a body nor present in one. The first two options have already been ruled out. So, they conclude, all these powers must come together in one thing that is neither bodily nor dependent on a body: the soul.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00225
I say that this argument does not help us solve the problem. Someone could reply: how do you know that the soul connects these powers?
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00226

If you mean only that the soul causes them to exist, that is not enough to show that the soul itself is the one that senses, nourishes, rests, writes, and laughs. Causing a power to exist does not make the powers work together or get in one another's way.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00227

If one cause creates separate powers in separate places and gives each its own tool, each power remains separate from the others and does not need them. How could one power's particular action stop another power from acting? You say that the Active Intellect is the source of every power in the body. Would that mean that all these powers help or hinder one another simply because they come from one source?
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00228

If by “connecting” the powers you mean that the soul itself sees what is visible, hears what is audible, and desires what is desirable—that the soul itself is the place where these powers are present and the source of their actions and qualities—then this is the truth, which nothing can overturn. But who has established this carefully and answered all the doubts that stand in its way?
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00229

If the soul itself does all these things, how can we still say that its powers are many and that they sometimes conflict? If they are one substance with one identity, this view also seems to undermine the separate powers that Avicenna and other philosophers place in different parts of the body. If the soul itself sees, hears, and desires, why claim that a seeing power is located in the spirit where the two optic nerves meet, or a hearing power in the spirit spread through the ear?
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00230
It would also mean that a person sees and hears through acts that belong to someone else, rather than through powers that belong to the person.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00231

There is a second way to say that the soul connects its powers. When the power of sight perceives a particular person, the rational soul recognizes that someone exists with this color, this shape, and this position. But it takes all these qualities in a general way. Even if we add a thousand general qualities to something general, it does not become a particular individual.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00232

The sense perception of that individual prepares the soul to know it in a general way. The soul's general understanding then prompts a general desire to obtain that thing. The desire becomes particular when it is received by a particular faculty. That particular desire is what we call appetite. The same explanation would apply to anger and the other particular states attributed to the human soul. This is the strongest account that can be given of the soul as a bond that gathers bodily powers, according to Avicenna and his followers.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00233

I say that this account also fails. The soul's relation to particular desires, anger, sensations, movements, and other individual states is not like the relation of one separate thing to another. It is not as though the soul understands, in a general way, everything that the other powers sense in a particular way. If that were so, the Active Intellect would also have desire, anger, sensation, and movement, just as a human being does. But we know that it is free of these concerns and reactions.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00234

We know directly that we are one self that thinks, senses, understands, moves, desires, becomes angry, and undergoes other reactions. The one in us that knows general truths is the same one that perceives particular things. The one that desires is the same one that becomes angry, and the same is true of other opposing qualities. This unity cannot be explained by a mere chain of relationships, like the relation between a ruler and soldiers or between a householder, children, and servants. We need a natural unity: one being with many different powers. This is known to those who have reached a deep understanding of the soul and its stages, and of the true existence and divine qualities made known through the names taught by God to Adam: “He taught Adam the names, all of them.” We have explained in several places that the stronger and simpler a being's existence is, the more meanings and effects it gathers within itself.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00235

There are three worlds: the world of intellect, the world of the animal soul, and the world of nature. The first is entirely free of multiplicity. The second is free of division into physical places and parts. The third is where multiplicity, conflict, and division among material things appear.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00236

The human soul, unlike other animal souls, has three levels: intellect and holiness, soul and imagination, and sense and nature. Every quality and action it has at one level is also present at the others, but in a way that fits each level.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00237

The senses and powers of perception and movement exist in the body as many separate powers because matter can be divided and can contain differences and opposites. The place of sight is not the place of hearing. Desire is not located where anger is, and the power for forceful movement is not in the same organ as the power for walking. One part of the body can feel the pain of a torn muscle while another feels the relief of a wound healing.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00238

All these powers also exist in the realm of imagination, the animal soul, as distinct powers, but they are united in one nonphysical field. There is no division into places as there is in the outer senses. An inner sense can see, hear, smell, taste, and touch particular things without splitting these acts among separate body parts. In the same way, it can desire, become angry, feel pain, and feel joy without bodily injury or healing. These powers are many in the world of the outer senses, but not divided by place in the world of inner sense.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00239

We also find all of them in the realm of intellect. There they are free of multiplicity, detail, physical division, and particular images, yet none of their meanings is missing. The intellectual human being is spiritual. All its parts are present in one being that is one in itself but rich in meaning. It has an intellectual face, sight, hearing, and limbs, all together without physical separation, as Aristotle explains in his Theology.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00240

You may ask: if the soul itself perceives everything and performs every action, why do we need many powers—some for perception, such as hearing and sight, and others for movement, such as attraction, repulsion, desire, and anger?
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00241

We answer: the soul is indeed all these powers. But for them to appear in the material world, they need separate bodily tools in different places. The bodily world is divided into parts. One physical organ, with one bodily nature, cannot give rise to many different qualities, such as hearing and seeing, or many different kinds of movement. The existence of an organ is not complete enough to gather all these meanings. A spiritual being, by contrast, can gather them within itself.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00242

The one soul is the source of every action carried out through its scattered powers and different organs, while remaining one in itself. In the same way, the one intellect gathers all the powers and meanings found in the other powers of the soul, senses, and body, but in a higher and more perfect way, as we have explained many times.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00243

You may also ask: how does the separate intellect differ from the soul in this ability to gather powers? The soul needs many different powers, bodily tools, and organs in order to express these qualities. Why does the intellect not need many materials and tools to carry out its actions and show its meanings?
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00244

We answer: the intellect gives its qualities to external matter by bringing things into being. It is not changed, affected, or made more complete by them. The soul, by contrast, cannot stand on its own or become free of change and reaction until it becomes pure intellect, with no lack or unrealized potential.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00245

Until then, the soul passes through different stages and needs all of them: sometimes it is at the level of sense and nature, sometimes at the level of soul and imagination, and sometimes at the level of intellect and what it understands. This is its condition as long as it is connected to the natural body. Once it leaves this world, it is at the level of separate intellect if it has reached full maturity in knowledge and action. If it has not, it remains at the second, imaginal level of the afterlife. There it takes on forms that fit its habits and states, which differ from one soul to another.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00246
VI. A weakness in the argument of the author of The Book of Discussions
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00247

As the light of truth has dawned on you from its horizon, as we have reminded you many times, consider the argument of one who argues for many sources of human actions, some bodily and some spiritual. The argument, in brief, is this: if the soul and its powers were one thing, the soul would have to be joined to matter when it nourishes the body, makes it grow, reproduces, and senses bodily things. Yet it would have to detach itself from matter when it understands abstract truths. But that is impossible.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00248
They argue also that if one power held all the images in its storehouse, it would always see them, as the intellect does when its knowledge is fully present.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00249

The author of The Book of Discussions answers that the imagination is bodily, as the ancient philosophers admit, though there are issues that do not fit our present discussion. The outer senses also play a part in imagination.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00250

As for the claim that the soul must mix with matter in order to nourish the body and do similar things, perhaps this does not follow. A being that is not joined to matter might still act on nourishment or other bodily processes in some way. Perhaps one power continues its work after another power stops. And perhaps reproduction and growth fail in certain people or at certain times because the body's mixture is no longer ready for them.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00251

For example, the balance of the spirits in the body's cavities can change, preparing different powers for different actions. A person's bodily mixture also changes with age, so it may become ready to receive many effects from one source, one effect from many sources, or one effect from one source in one particular way. The body may stop growing at a certain age even while the source of growth—the soul or intellect—remains.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00252

The argument goes on to say that certain actions attributed to these powers can come only from the Giver of Forms. If all forms come from that source and powers merely prepare the body to receive them, then perhaps readiness comes from powers that are not themselves living substances.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00253
That is the end of his statement.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00254

I see several problems with this argument. First, his agreement with the ancient philosophers that imagination is a bodily power is mistaken. As we have shown, imagination can exist apart from the natural body, even by the principles of those ancient philosophers.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00255

Second, it is wrong to allow that a separate soul could act on nourishment in a way that depends on nourishment to keep the soul itself alive. A separate being may govern lower things, but it is not changed or made more complete by them.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00256

Third, the claim that reproduction and growth stop at certain times because the body is no longer ready for them confuses the regular course of a kind of living thing with accidents that affect one individual. What belongs to a whole kind cannot be explained by the body's accidental conditions, because effects caused by those conditions would not happen always or even in most cases.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00257

The regular course shared by a whole kind comes from its active source. The fact that growth and reproduction stop with old age, and that natural death follows, is of this kind. These events come from causes that regularly lead to certain results: either directly, as when a soul reaches a new stage of completion, or indirectly, as when one power weakens because another has grown stronger, or when a soul turns away from one action in order to move toward another kind of life.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00258

As the soul enters a new life, it turns its power away from the bodily world, and the body dies as a result. You now know that each stage in the body's development follows the soul's progress through its own essential stages and changes. At each point, the soul has a different way of existing, and this brings with it a different action. The body's readiness follows the source that acts on it; it does not determine that source.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00259

An active source may remain while its effect is absent only when something blocks it. That happens rarely and by accident in a few individuals of a kind. It cannot explain why growth and reproduction regularly stop in old age, as they do in everyone. The fact that growth stops at that stage is therefore not caused by an accidental bodily obstacle.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00260

Another problem is the claim that actions come only from the Giver of Forms. This rests on the view that there are no substantial forms, a view we have already shown to be weak. The same is true of denying real powers. On the view we are criticizing, nourishment, growth, and reproduction in plants and animals come neither from their souls and powers nor from the human soul, but from a separate substance.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00261

We have explained in several places that the direct sources of motion and change are the natural powers present in bodies. The separate intellect is the source of all things, but it does not act on each one directly. The power of fire to heat and of water to cool, and other powers of this kind, are not merely conditions that prepare for an effect. They are true causes of the effects that regularly come from them.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00262
The same is true of the powers of plants and animals, as we explained in our discussion of forms. This is why we return to what we have said about the unity of the soul.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00263
VII. The body's powers are shadows of the soul's inner powers
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00264

Know that the powers present in the body and its organs belong to the natural human being. They are shadows and likenesses of the guiding soul and its powers—the human being of the next life. That imaginal human being, with its own powers and organs, is in turn a shadow and likeness of the intellectual human being, with its own aspects and qualities. The natural body, its organs, and its qualities are therefore shadows of shadows and likenesses of likenesses of what exists in the human intellect.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00265

The bodily powers of the natural human being are like an outer covering around the animal soul that will be raised in the next life, the true home of life. God says, “The home of the next life is truly life, if only they knew.” We can see this because when our outer powers and bodily senses fall quiet during sleep, illness, or other states, we often find that we can still hear, see, smell, touch, grasp, and walk. We have these senses and powers within us, without missing any of them. But they are not fixed in this world of outward sense and sight. If they were, everyone with sound senses would see them. Their true home is another world: the unseen world within the soul.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00266

The inward powers and tools are themselves shadows of what exists in the human intellect. The intellect is simple and undivided, yet it gives rise to these many powers in the soul and, through them, in the body. If it did not contain different aspects suited to its nature, one simple thing could not give rise to so many different things. Every high and noble being is the source, in a unified way, of the many meanings found in the beings below it.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00267

We have quoted the First Teacher, Aristotle, as saying plainly that the intellectual human being has all the organs of the human being who senses, but in a form that suits the intellect. Elsewhere he says that the bodily human being contains both the human soul and the intellectual human being. He does not mean that they are identical, but that the bodily human being is connected to them: it is an image of them. It carries out some actions of the intellectual human being and some of the animal soul. The bodily human being therefore gathers both kinds of meaning, though only weakly and in a limited way, since it is an image of an image.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00268

This shows that the first, higher human being does sense, but in a better and more complete way than the lower human being. The lower human being receives its senses from the higher, intellectual human being, as we have explained. This is a remarkable account of the force of Aristotle's insight into divine matters. He reached a height that later thinkers could not match. Most Muslim philosophers, including Avicenna and those like him, did not grasp what he meant. In The Healing, Avicenna dismissed the view he attributed to Plato and Socrates: that there are two human beings, one that perishes and one that is separate and everlasting. What would he have said if he had heard that every human being contains three beings, different in their degree of existence: a bodily being that perishes, an intellectual being that lasts, and an imaginal soul between them?
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00269

The bodily human form, with all its organs, is an image of the imaginal human being. The human being as it exists in the world of images is in turn an image of the human being understood through intellect. The imaginal human being is raised either among the happy, in Paradise, or among the miserable, in Hell. The intellectual human being, however, is in a seat of truth with a powerful King.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00270

The imaginal human being senses things and judges them through its own being, without using a bodily tool. It perceives things outside itself through images present within it. It perceives them through those very images; if it needed another image to perceive each image, this would lead to an endless chain. Its own being is sight for seeing, hearing for hearing, smell for smelling, taste for tasting, and touch for touching. As we have learned, the sense and the thing sensed are joined in the act of perception.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00271

The imaginal human being also judges things through its own being, whether these judgments come from imagination or another inner power. It desires what is pleasant and feels anger toward what conflicts with it. It does not need a separate desire or anger added to it. The same is true of the intellectual human being in all the corresponding ways.
Book Eight: Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00272

The greatest of the philosophers says: “These senses are weak intellects, and those intellects are strong senses.” Someone might object: if the human being in the higher world can sense, and sensation is what distinguishes animals, then sensation must be a reaction to a physical form. How can a noble, higher being have a sense that belongs to a lower one?
